abstract: Whey proteins, the most abundant proteins in human milk (HM), play a vital role in the growth and development of infants. This review first elaborates on the main components of HM whey proteins, including various proteins with specific functions, and details the functions of these proteins in terms of infant nutrition, immunity, as well as growth and development. Secondly, it analyzes factors that affect HM whey proteins, such as maternal differences, dietary habits, and geographical differences. Thirdly, it discusses detection methods for HM whey proteins, covering the principles, advantages, and limitations of different technical means. Finally, it compares whey proteins from different milk sources, highlighting their differences in composition, function, and characteristics. This review aims to comprehensively present the current research status of HM whey protein, provide a scientific basis for maternal and infant health, and contribute to optimizing infant feeding strategies and the research and development of related products.

HM whey protein detection methods
Recent research on HM whey proteins has led to the development of various analytical methods for qualitative and quantitative analyses. These methodologies involve proteomics, high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA), and capillary electrophoresis (CE), as summarized in

Each detection method offers distinct advantages and disadvantages, necessitating careful considerations of factors such as experimental purpose, sample properties, and experimental conditions to select the most suitable approach.

4.1
Proteomics technology
Proteomics is defined as the systematic isolation, identification, and characterization of proteins from certain sources. Proteomics technology has transformed cell biology and biochemistry, offering new powerful tools for studying complex protein groups, multiprotein complexes, and posttranslational modifications. Proteomics research employs two main strategies: “Top-down” technology, which involves treating and analyzing proteins in their intact form, and “Bottom-up” technology, in which proteins are extracted from samples and then enzymatically digested into shorter peptide segments for analysis (
Lenz & Dihazi, 2016
). Currently, the “Bottom-up” technology is the predominant method in whey protein research. From a technical perspective, proteomics combines two major techniques: separation and characterization.
Protein separation techniques include sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE), two-dimensional polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (2D-PAGE), and liquid-phase separation. Liquid-phase separation offers superior sensitivity, dynamic range, easier automation, and faster separation efficiency than SDS-PAGE and 2D-PAGE (
O'Donnell et al., 2004
). Liquid chromatography (LC) is the main liquid-phase separation technique used in proteomics. Different types of LC exist, and proteomic analysis often uses two or more types of LC, i.e., multidimensional LC, for separation. Nanoscale liquid chromatography is commonly used in LC-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) proteomics due to its excellent separation capability and efficiency (
Wei, 2018
).
Proteomic analyses primarily employ mass spectrometry (MS) to characterize proteins or peptides. Recent technological advancements in MS, such as Orbitrap MS, have substantially enhanced the resolving power of this technique, almost quadrupling the resolving power (
Wei, 2018
). Integration of S-lens ion optics, advanced active beam guide, and advanced quadrupole technology in the Q Exactive and Fusion series has boosted the sensitivity of MS 1 by over five times and MS 2 by over ten times (
Wei, 2018
). These technological advancements have allowed the accurate determination of the types and levels of various HM whey proteins, laying an important foundation for further exploration into their function and mechanisms.
LC-MS/MS can characterize a diverse array of proteins, which exhibit a wide range of physicochemical properties and molecular weights. Due to its unique advantages, LC-MS/MS has a broad range of applications, enabling the identification and analysis of multiple components within complex samples. Furthermore, its high sensitivity allows for the accurate detection of proteins even at minimal concentrations. Additionally, the structural analysis capabilities of LC-MS/MS are essential for identifying unknown components in complex samples. This technique aids researchers in gaining preliminary insights into the structural characteristics of these novel compounds, thereby providing a foundation for further separation and identification efforts (
Dai & Shen, 2022
). Table A.2 illustrates the application of proteomics techniques to detecting HM whey proteins in recent years. However, due to the high complexity of biological matrices, LC-MS/MS remains an imperfect technique. Analytes detected by LC-MS/MS can be influenced by matrix effects and ion suppression, which may adversely affect analytical performance (
Goff et al., 2020
). In addition, downstream data analysis related to LC-MS/MS remains a critical bottleneck (
Lu et al., 2022
). LC-MS/MS generates data containing thousands of protein signals, and extracting valuable information from this data—such as protein identification, quantification, and metabolic pathway analysis—presents a challenging task requiring operators to possess a solid understanding of bioinformatics.
4.2
High-performance liquid chromatography
HPLC plays a crucial role in the analysis of whey proteins in HM. It is frequently employed for qualitative and quantitative analysis of components within complex mixtures, as well as for preparative purposes. The separation of the sample is based on differences in migration rates through the column arising from different sample partitions between the stationary and mobile phases (
Ghanjaoui, 2020
). This separation capability enables the precise isolation of target proteins from complex mixtures of whey proteins in HM, thereby facilitating accurate quantitative analysis. This provides a reliable foundation for in-depth research on HM components and the development of related products. While HPLC possesses a certain degree of separation capability, it may lack the sensitivity required for detecting trace proteins. This limitation could result in the omission of critical low-abundance protein information when analyzing the complete profile of whey proteins in HM, thereby hindering a comprehensive understanding of the nutritional value and functional characteristics of HM. HPLC techniques commonly used for analyzing HM include hydrophilic interaction chromatography, ion exchange chromatography, reverse phase high-performance liquid chromatography (RP-HPLC), size-exclusion chromatography (SEC), and ultra-performance liquid chromatography (UPLC).
Santos and Ferreira (2007)
utilized RP-HPLC to quantitatively analyze α-lactalbumin in HM and revealed a gradual decrease in its content during lactation.
Yuan et al. (2021)
developed a novel two-step method for quantifying LF in HM. They first extracted LF using phosphate buffer (pH 5.0), purified it with a heparin affinity column, and then detected LF using UPLC at a wavelength of 201 nm. The detection and quantification limits were 1 and 5 mg/L, respectively, indicating that this method could be effectively used to quantify LF in HM. This method has the advantages of simplicity, low detection costs, and higher accuracy over previous HPLC methods.
Oberčkal et al. (2023)
used cation-exchange HPLC on a 0.1 mL weak cation exchange column CIMac™ COOH-0.1 to detect LF in HM. The analysis took approximately 7 min, but this time could be further shortened by using higher flow rates (up to 3 mL/min), and they detected LF concentrations ranging from 2.03 to 5.79 mg/mL in HM samples. The high density of positive charges on the LF N-terminal domain surface results in strong binding of LF to the column, with its elution occurring last during HM analysis. This approach confers high specificity to this method.
4.3
Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay
ELISA, an immunological assay, is based on the specific binding interaction between a target antigen and its corresponding antibodies and facilitates the quantitative analysis of specific proteins (antigens or biomarkers) in biological samples. ELISA offers exceptional sensitivity and specificity, enabling speedy and precise identification of target proteins, thereby ensuring the accuracy of the detection results. The drawbacks of ELISA include the high cost of specific antibodies, susceptibility to temperature variations and non-specific signals, which is one of the primary issues contributing to elevated limits of detection (
Wan et al., 2023
). ELISA comprises four main types: direct, indirect, sandwich, and competitive ELISA. Currently, various commercially available ELISA kits are commonly used to conduct experiments. These kits provide all necessary reagents, simplify sample preparation, require minimal sample size, and offer high accuracy, rendering them widely used.
Olivares et al. (2015)
used ELISA kits to quantify sIgA in the HM of 12 healthy mothers and 12 mothers with celiac disease (CD). They observed a significant decrease in sIgA content in the HM of mothers with CD compared to that of healthy mothers.
Dingess et al. (2021)
developed an ELISA method with high specificity for the quantitative analysis of sIgA in HM. This method employs the two-site “sandwich” technique, with two selected antibodies binding to human sIgA. Validated through MS, this method offers advantages over conventional serum IgA ELISA kits for sIgA detection.
Sha et al. (2020)
assessed the BSSL content in HM using a double-antibody sandwich ELISA technique and found a correlation between BSSL content, maternal BMI, and gestational diabetes mellitus.
Jiang and Lönnerdal (2019)
utilized ELISA kits to determine OPN levels in the HM of 12 healthy mothers over various postpartum periods: 1–14 days and 1, 2, 4, 6, and 12 months. The results unveiled that OPN was most concentrated in colostrum (178.0 ± 17.9 mg/L), with its concentrations gradually decreasing throughout the first year of lactation (48.3 ± 10.2 mg/L at 12 months postpartum).
Ruan et al. (2022)
also employed ELISA to determine OPN content in HM. The results showed average OPN levels of 343.2 ± 163.5 mg/L at 1–14 days, 228.4 ± 121.5 mg/L at 2–4 months, and 204.8 ± 100.6 mg/L at 5–7 months postpartum. OPN content peaked during the first 1–14 days postpartum and then declined. Some differences in the specific levels of OPN were observed between the two studies, but the overall trend remained consistent. Dynamic fluctuations in the concentration of OPN in HM indicate that infants require diverse amounts of OPN for growth and development at different stages of development.
4.4
Capillary electrophoresis
CE is a technique that separates proteins and peptides based on their charge-to-mass ratio, which is achieved by moving charged compounds inside a conductive solution under an applied potential. CE technology offers advantages such as small sample size, multiple separation modes, and high efficiency for protein analysis, with considerable application potential. However, protein adsorption to the capillary wall poses a significant challenge in CE, leading to changes in electroosmotic flow, peak broadening, and reduced separation efficiency. To mitigate this challenge, dynamic or static wall coatings are applied to the inner walls of the capillary, minimizing protein adsorption.
Puerta et al. (2023)
analyzed IgA in HM using capillary gel electrophoresis. They optimized the gel buffer and analyzed two types of IgA in less than 10 min using the short end of the capillary.
Yeh and Tseng (2012)
selectively extracted and enriched Lyz from HM using human serum albumin-modified gold nanoparticles, and analyzed it by CE, determining its concentration in HM to be 1.6 ± 0.2 μM.
4.5
Other detection methods
The diverse and abundant whey proteins in HM play a pivotal role in the growth and development of infants. Aside from the commonly used detection methods discussed above, alternative methods have also demonstrated efficacy. For example,
Zou et al. (2020)
developed a high-throughput fluorescence analytical method to detect LPO activity in human, bovine, goat, and camel milk. This method assesses LPO activity by monitoring the generation of red-fluorescent resorufin from LPO-catalyzed oxidation of Amplex® Red (1-(3,7-dihydroxyphenoxazin-10-yl)ethanone). The determined LPO activity in human, bovine, goat, and camel milk was 20.9, 4542, 1200, and 167 U/L, respectively.
Mukhametova et al. (2023)
employed a noncompetitive fluorescence polarization immunoassay with fluorescently labeled single-domain camelid antibodies to quantify LF content in HM. They obtained LF content values of 2.19 ± 0.02, 2.26 ± 0.14, 1.95 ± 0.05, and 1.85 ± 0.05 mg/mL in four HM samples.
